entry: World War I theater of operations between Russia and the [[Central Powers]], ranging from the [[Baltic Sea|Baltic Sea]] to the [[Black Sea|Black Sea]]. Unlike the static warfare on the [[Western Front (World War I)|Western Front]], fighting in the east was more dynamic, often involving the flanking and encirclement of entire formations. Russia's 1914 offensives did not achieve a rapid victory, and in 1915 Central Powers offensives reversed its gains in [[Galicia (Eastern Europe)|Galicia]] and Poland. To relieve pressure on France at the [[Battle of Verdun]], Russia attacked in 1916; its Brusilov offensive became the largest Entente victory of the war. After the February Revolution of 1917, the [[Bolsheviks]] overthrew the Russian Republic in the [[October Revolution]]. The Bolsheviks signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with the Central Powers in March 1918, taking Russia out of the war. The Armistice of 11 November 1918 annulled that treaty.

Venomous pit viper of the eastern United States, *Agkistrodon contortrix*. Its range runs from southern [[New England|New England]] to the [[Florida|Florida]] Panhandle and west to eastern [[Texas|Texas]] and parts of [[Kansas|Kansas]]. Adults usually measure 50–95 cm (20–37 in) including the tail. Dark brown, hourglass-shaped crossbands on a light reddish-brown or grayish background provide camouflage in leaf litter, and young snakes have green or yellow tail tips that darken within a year. The species favors deciduous and mixed woodlands and hibernates in dens or limestone crevices, often with timber rattlesnakes. It ambushes prey including insects and small mammals. Because it often freezes rather than fleeing, people may step on it, and copperhead bites account for half of the treated snake bites in the United States.

Tree squirrel native to eastern North America, *Sciurus carolinensis*. It is an ecologically essential natural forest regenerator in its native range, but it is regarded as an invasive species in Europe, where it has largely displaced the [[Red squirrel|red squirrel]] in Britain. Since 2016 the [[European Union|European Union]] has listed it as an invasive species of Union concern, barring its import, breeding, transport, sale and intentional release.

Umbrella term for cultures and nations, usually including Asia, the Arab world and, in historical contexts, the Mediterranean region. Originally a geographic term for the eastern part of the Old World, it contrasted the civilizations of Asia with those of [[Western Europe|Western Europe]]. The boundary between East and West is cultural and historical rather than geographical: [[Australia|Australia]] and New Zealand, founded as British settler colonies, are usually grouped with the Western world, while the Central Asian states of the former [[Soviet Union|Soviet Union]] are grouped with the East. Western scholarship in the tradition of Orientalism treated the East as one unified sphere covering all of Asia. Shared features include religions such as [[Buddhism|Buddhism]] and [[Hinduism|Hinduism]] and writing systems such as [[Chinese characters|Chinese characters]] and Brahmic scripts. Countries such as the [[Philippines|Philippines]] may be considered Western in some aspects of culture and politics because of influence from the [[United States|United States]] and Western Europe.

Ingestion of food for digestion. Heterotrophic organisms must ingest external organic matter to obtain the nutrients and energy needed for [[Metabolism|metabolism]] and growth. [[Carnivore|Carnivores]] and scavengers eat flesh, [[Herbivore|herbivores]] eat plants and algae, and omnivores eat both, while decomposers such as fungi digest food externally before absorbing nutrients. In humans, eating is organized into meals, routine sessions of cooked food, and [[Snack|snacks]], smaller casual servings often of non-staple food. Preparing and presenting meals is the craft of [[Culinary arts|culinary arts]]. Physicians consider a healthy diet essential, but intake may be reduced through dieting, religious [[Fasting|fasting]] or hunger strikes, and shortages can lead to starvation. Overeating may lead to [[Obesity|obesity]], which some public health professionals have declared an "obesity epidemic."

Mental disorder marked by abnormal eating behaviors that harm physical or mental health. Types include [[Anorexia|anorexia nervosa]], an intense fear of weight gain leading to food restriction and excessive exercise; [[Bulimia|bulimia nervosa]], in which binge eating is followed by purging; binge eating disorder, in which large amounts are eaten without hunger; and pica, the eating of nonfood items. [[Anxiety disorder|Anxiety disorders]], [[Depression (mood)|depression]] and substance abuse are common among those affected. Causes involve biological and environmental factors, and cultural idealization of thinness contributes to some cases. Treatment may involve counseling and dietary advice; about 70% of people with anorexia nervosa and 50% with bulimia recover within five years. Both anorexia and bulimia nervosa increase the risk of death.

American rapper, record executive and entrepreneur, dubbed the "Godfather of Gangsta Rap." He co-founded the group [[N.W.A|N.W.A]] and its label, Ruthless Records, established in 1987, which propelled West Coast and gangsta rap. Disputes over money split the group, and he became embroiled in rivalries with [[Ice Cube|Ice Cube]] and [[Dr. Dre|Dr. Dre]], who had left for solo careers. His solo releases included two EPs, and he signed and debuted the rap group Bone Thugs-n-Harmony. N.W.A was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame|Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2016, with Eazy-E posthumously.

Fictional protagonist of [[Charles Dickens|Charles Dickens]]'s 1843 novella *A Christmas Carol*. A cold-hearted miser who despises [[Christmas|Christmas]], Scrooge is visited by the ghost of his late partner Jacob Marley and by three spirits, and he is transformed into a better, more generous man. His surname has become a byword for greed and misanthropy, and his catchphrase "Bah! Humbug!" is often used to express disgust with modern Christmas traditions.

Ancient kingdom in [[Syria|Syria]], whose remains form a tell about 55 km (34 mi) southwest of [[Aleppo|Aleppo]]. Settled around 3500 BC, Ebla became a trading empire and later an expansionist power that dominated much of northern and eastern Syria. It was destroyed in the 23rd century BC, rebuilt, and finally destroyed by the Hittite king Mursili I in c. 1600 BC. Its trade network reached [[Sumer|Sumer]], [[Cyprus|Cyprus]], [[Egypt|Egypt]] and as far as Afghanistan. Excavation from 1964 showed that the [[Levant|Levant]] was a center of ancient civilization equal to Egypt and Mesopotamia. The archive of about 20,000 [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]] tablets, dated to 2500–2350 BC, is written in Sumerian and in the Eblaite language, and it has clarified Sumerian and Levantine social customs of the mid-3rd millennium BC.

Zoonotic viral hemorrhagic fever in humans and other primates, caused by four of the six known ebolaviruses. Symptoms usually begin 2 to 21 days after infection with fever, sore throat, muscle pain and headache, followed by vomiting, [[Diarrhea|diarrhea]], rash and, in some cases, [[Bleeding|internal and external bleeding]]. Outbreaks have had mortality rates of 25–90%, averaging about 50%, and death often results from shock due to fluid loss. The virus spreads through direct contact with body fluids, and no airborne spread between humans or other primates has been documented. Fruit bats are believed to be the natural host. Symptoms may resemble those of [[Malaria|malaria]] or [[Cholera|cholera]], so diagnosis relies on testing blood for viral RNA, antibodies or the virus itself. Two treatments have been shown to improve outcomes, and an Ebola vaccine was approved in the United States in December 2019.

Spiny, egg-laying [[Monotreme|monotreme]] mammal of the family Tachyglossidae, native to [[Australia|Australia]] and [[New Guinea|New Guinea]]. Four species are recognized, and together with the [[Platypus|platypus]] they are the only living mammals that lay eggs. Echidnas are covered in hollow, keratin spines and have toothless jaws and long, sticky tongues that take ants, termites and [[Earthworm|earthworms]]. Their elongated snouts carry electroreceptors for finding burrowing prey; the long-beaked echidna has about 2,000, against 40,000 on the platypus's bill. They are powerful diggers and capable swimmers. Females lay a single leathery egg and incubate it in a temporary pouch. Echidnas evolved between 20 and 50 million years ago from platypus-like ancestors.

Marine animal of the phylum Echinodermata, including [[Starfish|starfish]], brittle stars, [[Sea urchin|sea urchins]] and [[Sea cucumber|sea cucumbers]]. Adults are usually recognizable by five-pointed radial symmetry, although their larvae are bilaterally symmetrical. The phylum contains about 7,600 living species, the second-largest group of deuterostomes after the [[Chordate|chordates]] and the largest marine-only phylum. Echinoderms occur on the seabed at every ocean depth. Most can regenerate tissue, organs and limbs, and in some cases a complete animal regenerates from a single limb. Their ossified dermal endoskeletons contribute to many [[Limestone|limestone]] formations and provide clues to ancient environments. Echinoderms were the most used species in regenerative research in the 19th and 20th centuries. The first definitive echinoderms appeared near the start of the [[Cambrian|Cambrian]].

Astronomical event in which an object is temporarily obscured by passing into another body's shadow or between it and the viewer. An eclipse results from an occultation (complete hiding) or a transit (partial hiding). The term most often describes a [[Solar eclipse|solar eclipse]], when the shadow of the [[Moon|Moon]] crosses [[Earth|Earth]], or a [[Lunar eclipse|lunar eclipse]], when the Moon enters Earth's shadow. Eclipses also occur between planets and moons, and in [[Binary star|binary star]] systems whose orbits intersect the observer's position. Solar and lunar eclipses happen only during eclipse seasons, when the orbital planes of Earth and the Moon line up near the [[Sun|Sun]]. The word derives from the [[Ancient Greek|Ancient Greek]] ékleipsis, meaning 'abandonment' or 'darkening of a heavenly body'.

Apparent path of the [[Sun|Sun]] on the [[Celestial sphere|celestial sphere]], resulting from Earth's orbit around the Sun. The ecliptic was central to ancient astronomy, astrology and calendar-making, and it is named for the observation that [[Eclipse|eclipses]] occur only when the Moon crosses it. The planets of the [[Solar System|Solar System]] appear along the ecliptic because their orbits lie close to Earth's plane. The Moon's orbit is inclined only 5.1°, and it intersects the ecliptic at the lunar nodes. Ancient scientists calculated Earth's [[Axial tilt|axial tilt]] by comparing the ecliptic, about 23.4°, with the equatorial plane. The ecliptic is the basis of the ecliptic coordinate system, and it is used as the reference plane of the Solar System, though the invariable plane is more precisely defined.

Concept in ecology describing the specific environmental conditions a species or population occupies. The term was coined in 1910 by Roswell Hill Johnson. Joseph Grinnell first used it in research in 1917, defining a niche by the [[Habitat|habitat]] a species lives in and its accompanying behavioral adaptations. In 1927 Charles Sutherland Elton emphasized the role a species plays in its biotic environment and its use of resources. G. Evelyn Hutchinson defined the niche in 1957 as the set of environmental variables and their ranges within which a species can persist. In niche theory, species with overlapping niches should [[Competition (biology)|compete]], and coexistence requires differences between their niches. The concept is central to ecological biogeography, which studies spatial patterns of [[Ecology|ecological]] communities.

Application of statistical methods to economic data to give empirical content to economic relationships. A basic tool is the multiple linear regression model, still the most frequently used starting point for an analysis. Econometric theory develops estimators with desirable properties such as unbiasedness, efficiency and consistency, while applied econometrics uses data to assess economic theories, develop models, analyze economic history and forecast. Its origins lie in the [[Least squares|least squares]] method of the early 19th century, first used in astronomy and geodesy. In 1889 the British statistician Udny Yule applied [[Linear regression|linear regression]] to public assistance and poverty in England. Logistic regression emerged in the 1940s, and in the 1980s improved computing enabled nonlinear methods such as [[Neural network (machine learning)|artificial neural networks]]. Jan Tinbergen and Ragnar Frisch are the two founding fathers of the field; Frisch coined the term in the sense used today.

Increase in the quantity and quality of the goods and services a society produces, usually measured as the inflation-adjusted growth of [[Gross domestic product|gross domestic product]] or GDP per capita. Growth from more efficient use of inputs is called intensive; growth from larger inputs, such as a bigger population or new territory, is extensive. Increases in labor productivity have historically been the most important source of real per capita growth. Economist Robert Solow concluded that technological progress accounted for 80 percent of the long-term rise in U.S. per capita income. Over the 20th century the real price of many goods fell by over 90%. Before the [[Industrial Revolution|Industrial Revolution]], technological progress raised population rather than income, a condition known as the Malthusian trap.

Distribution of income, wealth or consumption among individuals or groups within or between nations. Income inequality is measured by metrics such as the [[Gini coefficient|Gini coefficient]], a scale from 0 for perfect equality to 1 for maximal inequality, and by the inequality-adjusted [[Human Development Index|Human Development Index]]. Over the long run inequality has tended to rise, with declines during the two World Wars and after the creation of postwar [[Welfare state|welfare states]]. Globalization reduced inequality between nations but increased it within most, particularly in advanced countries. Research has linked inequality to political instability, democratic breakdown and civil conflict, and suggests that it hinders [[Economic growth|growth]]. Government tax and spending policies have significant effects on income distribution.

Set of government actions that set taxation, budgets, the money supply, interest rates and labor market regulation. Most instruments are divided into fiscal policy, which concerns government revenue and spending, and monetary policy, which concerns central bank actions on the money supply and interest rates. Mercantilism dominated European states from the 17th century until it was challenged by [[Adam Smith|Adam Smith]]. The [[Great Depression|Great Depression]] discredited laissez-faire orthodoxy and gave rise to Keynesian demand management, which came under attack during the stagflation of the 1970s. After the [[2008 financial crisis|2008 financial crisis]] and the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020, governments intervened on a scale not seen since the postwar era. Policy goals often conflict: policies that reduce unemployment can raise inflation.

Socialist market economy of the People's Republic of China, the second-largest by nominal [[Gross domestic product|GDP]]. It has been the largest by purchasing power parity since 2016, and China accounted for 19% of the global economy in 2025 in PPP terms. State-owned and mixed-ownership enterprises operate alongside a large private sector that contributes about 60% of GDP and 90% of new jobs. China is the world's largest manufacturer, and its production exceeds that of the nine next largest manufacturers combined. Manufacturing is shifting toward electric vehicles and [[Renewable energy|renewable energy]]. Market reforms introduced under [[Deng Xiaoping|Deng Xiaoping]] in 1978 opened the economy to foreign investment. Growth has faced challenges in the 2020s from a property crisis.

Developing market-oriented economy with substantial state participation in strategic sectors. In October 2026 India was the sixth-largest economy by nominal [[Gross domestic product|GDP]] and the third-largest by [[Purchasing power parity|purchasing power parity]]. Domestic consumption generates nearly 70% of GDP, and services account for around 55%. Protectionist policies and central planning lasted from independence in 1947 until a balance-of-payments crisis in 1991 led to broad liberalization. India has been a member of the [[World Trade Organization|WTO]] since 1995.

Combined economies of the member states of the [[European Union|European Union]], forming a single internal market. The EU is the second-largest economy by nominal GDP after the United States and the third-largest by [[Purchasing power parity|purchasing power parity]], generating one-sixth of global output. Germany, France, Italy and Spain are the four largest economies. Most member states use the [[Euro|euro]], the second most-traded reserve currency after the [[United States dollar|United States dollar]]. Services make up 64.7% of GDP, manufacturing 23.8% and agriculture 1.5%. Starting with [[Greece|Greece]] in 2009, several eurozone states needed bailouts during the European debt crisis, and all had exited their programs by the late 2010s. [[Paris|Paris]] is the economically strongest city in the EU.

Highly developed, diversified market-oriented economy, the world's largest by nominal [[Gross domestic product|GDP]]. It generates about 26% of global output and is the second-largest by [[Purchasing power parity|purchasing power parity]]. Consumer spending has comprised over 60% to 70% of the economy since the 1990s. The nation is the second-largest manufacturer, with about a fifth of global manufacturing. In the 1820s and 1830s [[Mass production|mass production]] shifted much of the economy from artisans to factories. Since [[World War II|World War II]] the economy has achieved relatively steady growth, low unemployment and low inflation. The [[New York Stock Exchange|New York Stock Exchange]] and [[Nasdaq|Nasdaq]] are the world's largest stock exchanges by market capitalization. Its largest trading partners are [[Mexico|Mexico]], [[Canada|Canada]], China, Japan and Germany.

Complication of pregnancy in which the [[Embryo|embryo]] attaches outside the [[Uterus|uterus]], most often in a fallopian tube. Symptoms classically include abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding, and the [[Fetus|fetus]] cannot survive. Risk factors include [[Chlamydia|chlamydia]] infection, [[Smoking|smoking]] and [[Endometriosis|endometriosis]]. Diagnosis relies on blood tests for human chorionic gonadotropin and on ultrasound. Surgery removes the embryo or the tube, though methotrexate can work when hormone levels are low and the ectopic is small. It is the most common cause of death among women in the first trimester.

Country in northwestern [[South America|South America]], bordered by [[Colombia|Colombia]] to the north and [[Peru|Peru]] to the east and south. It includes the [[Galápagos Islands|Galápagos Islands]], about 1,000 km west of the mainland. Indigenous peoples were gradually incorporated into the [[Inca Empire|Inca Empire]] in the 15th century, and the territory was colonized by the [[Spanish Empire|Spanish Empire]] in the 16th century. Ecuador became independent in 1820 as part of Gran Colombia and emerged as a sovereign state in 1830. Its capital is [[Quito|Quito]], and the largest city is [[Guayaquil|Guayaquil]]. Most of its 17.8 million people are mestizos. The 2008 constitution was the first in the world to recognize legally enforceable rights of nature.
